title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction
authors: Wen-Chuang Shang, Chenyu Shen, Mikito Tsujimoto, Tomonori Tanaka, Yoshihiro Gohda
abstract: We introduce GMMag, a workflow for generating crystal structures together with their site-resolved magnetic moments, built on a conditional variational autoencoder with a graph neural network encoder and a transformer decoder. Gaussian-mixture sampling redirects generation towards selected chemical and magnetic targets without retraining. We systematically investigate how encoder and decoder design, the representation of magnetic-moment magnitudes and relative signs, and sampling choices affect reconstruction, generation quality and diversity. Because a higher screening pass rate does not necessarily yield more qualifying candidates with distinct chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, we model how repeated generation of the same chemical formulas limits their accumulation and test the model in two separate ten-million-draw runs. As an application, the workflow identifies Nd-containing candidates with chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.

infographic.key_insight: GMMag generates crystal structures with site-resolved magnetic moments and uses Gaussian-mixture sampling to steer outputs toward chemical and magnetic targets without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports magnetic-material candidate discovery while estimating how repeated chemical formulas limit distinct-candidate yield under a finite generation budget.
method: Combine a graph neural network encoder and transformer decoder in a conditional variational autoencoder.
Retarget generation through Gaussian-mixture sampling and compare magnetic-moment representations and model designs.
Model accumulation of qualifying candidates with distinct chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: The yield model was tested in two separate ten-million-draw runs, and an application identified Nd-containing candidates with reference-absent formulas, negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.
infographic.watch_item: A higher screening pass rate may not produce more distinct qualifying formulas; reported candidates and estimated magnetization still require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction

title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene
authors: Djardiel S. Gomes, Isaac M. Félix, Marcelo L. Pereira Junior
abstract: Opening a band gap in metallic two-dimensional carbon allotropes is an important step toward their use in electronic and optoelectronic devices, and full hydrogenation has proven to be an effective route to achieve it. Here, we propose irida-graphane, the fully hydrogenated derivative of the irida-graphene, a monolayer composed of three-, six-, and eight-membered rings, and investigate its structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory (DFT) at the PBE and HSE06 levels combined with phonon and \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. All carbon atoms adopt $sp^3$ hybridization, with the hydrogen atoms of the three- and six-membered rings bonded to opposite sides of a buckled carbon framework, and the lattice parameter contracts by 4.3% with respect to irida-graphene. The hydrogenation energy of $-0.53$ eV/H indicates that the hydrogenation of irida-graphene from molecular hydrogen is exothermic. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies confirms the dynamical stability of irida-graphane, and AIMD simulations show that its structure remains intact at temperatures up to 2000 K. Irida-graphane is mechanically isotropic, with an in-plane stiffness of approximately 156 N/m, a Poisson's ratio of approximately 0.1, and critical strains of approximately 20%. Hydrogenation transforms the metallic parent structure into a semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 4.68 eV (PBE) and 6.0 eV (HSE06). Irida-graphane is transparent in the visible range, with reflectivity below 0.3%, and absorbs strongly in the deep ultraviolet, with absorption coefficients of the order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ cm$^{-1}$. These results suggest irida-graphane as a candidate wide-gap material for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.

infographic.key_insight: Full hydrogenation converts metallic irida-graphene into irida-graphane, a predicted wide-gap semiconductor with a 6.0 eV indirect band gap at the HSE06 level.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicted visible transparency and strong deep-ultraviolet absorption make irida-graphane a candidate for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.
method: PBE and HSE06 density functional theory calculations
Phonon analysis and ab initio molecular dynamics
Structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical characterization
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations predict no imaginary phonon frequencies, structural integrity in AIMD simulations up to 2000 K, visible reflectivity below 0.3%, and deep-UV absorption coefficients of 10⁵–10⁶ cm⁻¹.

title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning
authors: Mingkang Liu, Zhanghao Zhouyin, Guanghui Wang, Daye Zheng, Lei Shen, Qiangqiang Gu
abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) gives the electronic structure of materials, but its cost limits large-supercell calculations and materials screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonians bypass the self-consistent cycle but are usually system-specific; universal ones could cover new compositions and disordered solids. Such models must generalize across chemistry and keep downstream properties physical, while staying inexpensive for large cells. Here we introduce UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors rooted in density-functional tight-binding theory with deep learning. UniTB's network, which corrects a prior Hamiltonian, generalizes across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding. A projection bounds band shifts from the prior, suppressing spurious states and keeping downstream properties physical. We provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. The variant UniTB-Flash assembles its prior from two-center tables at $O(N)$ cost for $N$ atoms, against $O(N\log N)$ on a grid. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements. Without amorphous training data, both models agree with DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te. UniTB-Flash ranks candidates with no significant difference from UniTB, whose property values are more accurate; together they screen 16,195 crystals for five application domains of industrial relevance.

infographic.key_insight: UniTB combines physical priors with equivariant deep learning to predict electronic Hamiltonians across diverse chemistries while constraining unphysical band shifts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its fast Hamiltonian predictions support large-cell electronic-property calculations and materials screening, with UniTB-Flash offering linear-cost prior assembly.
method: Learn corrections to a density-functional tight-binding prior using an E(3)-equivariant network.
Use prior-routed mixture-of-experts learning and a charge-equilibration head to generalize across chemistry.
Bound band shifts through projection; accelerate computation with SO(2) GPU kernels and two-center tables in UniTB-Flash.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB achieves 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements; both variants reproduce DFT optics and conductivity for amorphous Ge-Sb-Te without amorphous training data.
infographic.watch_item: UniTB-Flash preserves candidate rankings in the reported evaluation but yields less accurate property values than UniTB.
infographic.paper_title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning

title: HorizON: A Multi-Horizon Deep Operator Network for Property Prediction of Organic Battery Stacks
authors: Subhash V. S. Ganti, Lukas Woelfel, Arla Diengdoh, Tzvetan Mihaylov, Thomas Nevolianis, Jan Meyer
abstract: Transition-metal-based batteries rely on critical elements such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Their extraction creates environmental and supply-chain challenges. Organic electrode materials (OEMs) reduce this reliance and provide broad molecular tunability. However, OEM-based batteries still show limited long-term cycling stability. Their design also requires the joint optimization of coupled metrics such as voltage, specific capacity, capacity retention, and energy density. These metrics depend on the full battery stack and on the interactions among its components rather than on the active material alone. In our previous work, we developed a data-fusion multi-task framework for average discharge voltage and first-cycle specific capacity. Both targets are single-valued. Here, we extend that framework to multi-horizon prediction by predicting a property at every cycle of a discharge trajectory rather than at a single cycle. Our multi-fidelity and Multi-horizon Deep Operator Network learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories within one model. We train it on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions, so it learns battery-stack interactions rather than cathode-only effects. This framework supports long-term property prediction, inverse design, and process optimization for organic battery systems.

infographic.key_insight: HorizON jointly learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories from full organic battery-stack representations and usage conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting capacity across cycling could support organic battery-stack design and process optimization beyond single-cycle performance.
method: Uses a multi-fidelity, multi-horizon Deep Operator Network.
Learns DFT redox potentials and capacity trajectories within one model.
Represents the complete battery stack and usage conditions to capture component interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes training on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions but reports no dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy at long cycling horizons and generalization to unseen stack configurations remain unquantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: HorizON: A Multi-Horizon Deep Operator Network for Property Prediction of Organic Battery Stacks

title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in α-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers
authors: Junting Zhang, Andrew P. Horsfield, Mark R. Wenman
abstract: Zr cladding alloys in nuclear reactors are exposed to high neutron fluxes, making irradiation-induced defects and solute segregation central to understanding their in-service behaviour. Dislocation cores involve short-range chemistry and long-range elastic fields, which are difficult to describe simultaneously using conventional atomistic methods. Using a hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning (QM/ML) framework, this part of work examines prismatic <a> loops in hcp α-Zr. All three loop variants are considered, including faulted and perfect, interstitial- and vacancy-type, and first- and second-order prismatic configurations. Nine possible dislocation line segments are characterised in terms of core geometry, solute binding, glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transition pathways using QM/ML and newly implemented QM/ML-NEB calculations. Shockley and half-Shockley partials, together with basal and prismatic fault ribbons, are found to govern core stabilisation. Fe and H preferentially bind to faulted segments, whereas Sn and Nb favour perfect segments. Solutes can also drive partial motion, recombination and local unfaulting. These results establish a comprehensive picture of <a> loop microstructure, solute trapping and transition mechanisms in α-Zr.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid QM/ML calculations reveal how partial dislocations and fault ribbons stabilise prismatic <a> loops in α-Zr, with Fe and H favouring faulted segments and Sn and Nb favouring perfect segments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings can inform models of solute trapping and irradiation-induced microstructure evolution in zirconium nuclear fuel cladding.
method: Hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning modelling of dislocation cores.
Characterisation of nine line segments across three prismatic <a> loop variants.
QM/ML-NEB calculations of glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transition pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports core geometries, solute-binding preferences and transition mechanisms across nine dislocation line segments, but provides no numerical barriers or validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability from local segment calculations to evolving loops under reactor irradiation remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in α-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers

title: Learning the Chronology of Materials Discovery for Synthesizability Prediction
authors: Junkil Park, Aron Walsh
abstract: High-throughput computational and generative approaches are proposing candidate materials far faster than they can be synthesized, making it increasingly important to identify which hypothetical materials are likely to be experimentally realizable. Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning has emerged as a representative framework for synthesizability prediction, yet existing approaches treat experimentally reported materials as a static collection, overlooking the historical trajectory of materials discovery and the diverse practical factors that have driven its progress. Here we introduce ChronoSyn, a chronology-aware machine learning model that jointly learns synthesizability and the relative reporting order of known materials through a shared composition representation. Incorporating discovery chronology provides additional supervision beyond conventional synthesizability labels, improving prediction performance and enabling ChronoSyn to identify experimentally realizable compositions more effectively than baseline models. Applied to approximately 50 million hypothetical compositions, ChronoSyn identifies chemically coherent high-scoring families that include experimentally reported compositions unseen during training. These results highlight the chronology of materials discovery as an informative learning signal and suggest that the path along which known materials were discovered can point the way to those that will be discovered in the future.

infographic.key_insight: ChronoSyn uses the chronology of materials discovery as an additional learning signal to improve predictions of which hypothetical compositions are experimentally realizable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could help prioritize synthesis candidates from large computational and generative materials libraries.
method: Learn a shared representation of material composition.
Jointly predict synthesizability and the relative reporting order of known materials.
Score hypothetical compositions to identify promising chemical families.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved prediction over baseline models and screening of approximately 50 million hypothetical compositions, with high-scoring families containing experimentally reported compositions unseen during training.
infographic.watch_item: Reporting chronology may reflect research priorities and historical biases as well as synthesis feasibility; prospective experimental validation is not described in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the Chronology of Materials Discovery for Synthesizability Prediction

title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
authors: Yue Wu, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

infographic.key_insight: Retention-constrained fine-tuning improves aluminium MACE defect predictions while preserving the tested near-equilibrium mechanical and vibrational response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The protocol supports more reliable atomistic simulations of defect dynamics and plasticity without sacrificing validated bulk behaviour.
method: Acquire configurations using conditional force uncertainty from sensitivities over 144 readout weights.
Iteratively update all model parameters with relative-energy anchoring to retain historical behaviour.
Gate updates against historical elastic-group energy and vibrational tolerances.

infographic.watch_item: Retention is demonstrated only for the tested aluminium configurations and tolerances; deployment requires compatible reference energies and acceptance checks.
infographic.paper_title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity

title: From Autonomous Knowledge Generation to Generalizable Property Prediction: A Precision-First Pipeline for Electro-Optic Materials Discovery
authors: Dibakar Datta
abstract: Electro-optic materials, whose refractive index changes linearly with an applied electric field (the Pockels effect), set the speed and energy of optical modulators and microwave-to-optical links for quantum computing. Designing better materials requires optimizing composition alongside temperature, strain, and bias field. However, general repositories lack electro-optic tensor data. We present a pipeline that builds such a database from literature following the rule: "no value is better than a wrong value." The pipeline has five stages: physics-aware acquisition, layout-aware extraction via LLM and deterministic table parsers, a three-tier verification gate, cross-paper consensus using median and median absolute deviation, and a noise-robust surrogate model audited by leave-one-material-out (LOMO) testing. Physics enters directly: notation is mapped, point-group symmetry-forbidden Pockels components are rejected, equivalent labels are merged, and values carry provenance tags. In a run over 49 publications, the gate processed 816 candidates into 414 accepted, 215 held for review, and 187 rejected. Against a hand-certified gold standard of 303 values from 16 papers, the run achieved a precision of 0.51 and recall of 0.48 for exact record matches. Across four database snapshots, held-out materials where the surrogate model beat a predict-the-mean baseline grew from 1 of 4 to 9 of 13 as the database expanded from 10 to 22 materials. While not a controlled comparison, this trend supports the premise that a precision-oriented, physics-checked database can power forward models beyond its training set and clarifies requirements for inverse material design.

infographic.key_insight: A precision-first, physics-checked literature pipeline builds electro-optic datasets that support property prediction for unseen materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could guide electro-optic material selection for optical modulators and quantum microwave-to-optical links.
method: Acquire relevant papers and extract values using layout-aware LLMs and deterministic table parsers.
Apply three-tier verification, symmetry checks, notation normalization, and provenance tracking.

infographic.watch_item: Moderate exact-match accuracy warrants continued curation, and the uncontrolled snapshot comparison does not establish that database expansion caused prediction gains.
infographic.paper_title: From Autonomous Knowledge Generation to Generalizable Property Prediction: A Precision-First Pipeline for Electro-Optic Materials Discovery

title: First-principles-based search for emergent topological spin textures in transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers
authors: Yuhyun Cha, Do Hoon Kiem, Myung Joon Han
abstract: Topological spin textures such as skyrmions and bimerons offer rich physical functionalities and strong potential for future spin-based technologies. Identifying materials that host such emergent magnetic states, however, remains challenging due to the complex interplay between microscopic magnetic interactions and large-scale spin textures. Here, using a multiscale first-principles discovery framework, we identify a broad class of two-dimensional materials that stabilize nontrivial spin textures. The framework integrates relativistic density functional theory, magnetic force theory, and atomistic spin-dynamics simulations, enabling a direct connection between electronic interactions and emergent magnetic textures and allowing efficient screening of systems with large magnetic unit cells and competing exchange interactions. Applying this approach, we systematically screen 312 monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides across 1T and 2H phases of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals. We uncover a diverse set of emergent spin textures, including skyrmions, bimerons, and complex domain states, and clarify their distinct stabilization mechanisms driven by exchange interactions, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, and magnetic frustration. These results identify promising candidate materials for topological spin textures and establish a transferable computational framework for accelerating materials discovery of complex magnetic states in two dimensions.

infographic.key_insight: A first-principles multiscale search identifies monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides that support skyrmions, bimerons, and complex magnetic domain states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These candidate two-dimensional magnets could guide materials selection for future spin-based devices.

Extract microscopic magnetic interactions using magnetic force theory.

infographic.watch_item: Experimental realization and device-relevant thermal stability are not established in the abstract.

title: Oxygen partial pressure induced dielectric phase evolution in PLD deposited Barium Strontium Titanate thin films
authors: Shashi Pandey, Suk Hyun Sung, Jacob Fernandez, John T. Heron
abstract: Barium Strontium Titanate ((BaxSr1-x)TiO3, BST) thin films are amongst the most extensively studied dielectric alloys over the last decade. This is due to the tunability of the dielectric constant and dissipation factor in the underlying ferroelectric and paraelectric states. One important feature of BST is that the competition between the ferroelectric BaTiO3 and the paraelectric SrTiO3 parent phases can be tuned by the A-site alloy concentration, opening a platform for exploring dielectric phase competition. However, the understanding of the interplay between and establishing the control of the dielectric phase from thin film deposition parameters has not been sufficiently reported in the literature. Here, we synthesized a series of SrRuO3/BST/SrRuO3 epitaxial thin film heterostructures by Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) from a (Ba0.9Sr0.1)TiO3 target under systematic variation of the oxygen partial pressure during the BST deposition. We mapped the dielectric phase of the film to the oxygen growth pressure, film composition, and film crystal structure. A ferroelectric, relaxor-like, or paraelectric phase can be obtained with relatively moderate change in oxygen growth pressure. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis further indicates that this pressure-dependent phase evolution is accompanied by a structural transition of the BST lattice from tetragonal toward a nearly cubic phase, with the latter corresponding to the relaxor-like state. The control of the dielectric phase opens a pathway to study phase evolution and enable future computing technologies.

infographic.key_insight: Varying oxygen pressure during BST thin-film growth produces ferroelectric, relaxor-like, or paraelectric behavior, linking deposition conditions to dielectric phase.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Oxygen growth pressure offers a fabrication control for engineering dielectric states in epitaxial BST devices relevant to future computing technologies.
method: Deposit SrRuO3/BST/SrRuO3 epitaxial heterostructures by pulsed laser deposition using a (Ba0.9Sr0.1)TiO3 target.
Systematically vary oxygen partial pressure during BST growth.
Map dielectric phase against growth pressure, film composition, and crystal structure; examine lattice changes using STEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three dielectric states across moderate pressure changes and STEM evidence of a tetragonal-to-nearly-cubic structural transition, with the nearly cubic lattice corresponding to relaxor-like behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical pressure window, dielectric performance metrics, or reproducibility data to guide process transfer.
infographic.paper_title: Oxygen partial pressure induced dielectric phase evolution in PLD deposited Barium Strontium Titanate thin films

title: Spin-Charge Conversion in an Epitaxial Kagome Flat-Band Metal
authors: Wenyi Zhou, Yuqing Zhu, Katherine Johnson, Hari Paudyal, Duy Nguyen, Dimitri King
abstract: The formation of topological flat bands near the Fermi level in kagome-structured metals has generated substantial research interest. One key consequence of this electronic structure is the strong anisotropy in charge transport, such as the significantly higher in-plane resistivity relative to the out-of-plane direction. However, the spin transport properties of these flat-band kagome metals are still largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate spin-charge conversion in CoSn, a representative flat-band kagome metal. Scanning tunneling microscopy is employed to image the CoSn surface with atomic resolution, and $dI/dV$ spectroscopy shows clear signatures of the flat bands. Using magneto-optical techniques, we quantify the spin-orbit torque (SOT) in bilayers of ferromagnetic nickel (Ni) and c-plane CoSn thin films. We find a large effective spin Hall angle of $θ_{SH} = 0.484 \pm 0.005$ within the CoSn layers, significantly exceeding the value measured for Pt of $θ_{SH} = 0.0436 \pm 0.0003$ in Ni/Pt bilayers. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations provide a microscopic understanding of the intrinsic spin Hall effect in CoSn, elucidating the sources of Berry curvature in momentum space. These findings establish kagome metals as promising materials for efficient spin-charge conversion and low-power spintronics.

infographic.key_insight: Epitaxial kagome CoSn exhibits efficient spin-charge conversion, with an effective spin Hall angle about 11 times that of the measured Pt reference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CoSn could enable more efficient spin-orbit-torque devices for low-power spintronics.
method: Atomic-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and dI/dV spectroscopy probe CoSn surfaces and flat-band signatures.
Magneto-optical measurements quantify spin-orbit torque in Ni/CoSn and reference Ni/Pt bilayers.
DFT calculations investigate intrinsic spin Hall physics and momentum-space Berry curvature.
infographic.evidence_signal: The reported effective spin Hall angle is 0.484 ± 0.005 for CoSn versus 0.0436 ± 0.0003 for Pt in the measured bilayers.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish device-level switching energy or how performance varies with film orientation, thickness, and interface quality.
infographic.paper_title: Spin-Charge Conversion in an Epitaxial Kagome Flat-Band Metal

title: No Value Is Better Than a Wrong Value: Finding and Handling Erroneous Data in Literature-Mined Datasets for AI
authors: Achyut Manoj, Advai Aiyer, Andrew Lee, Nayan Saini, Pragya Birla, Dibakar Datta
abstract: Machine learning across materials science, chemistry, energy, and medicine increasingly relies on literature-extracted datasets due to a lack of curated databases. However, automated extraction introduces errors: text recognition misreads digits, units and notations are confused, values are misattributed, and LLMs hallucinate numbers. Drawing on our work building an electro-optic property database, we present a taxonomy of errors organized by their origin and signatures, alongside a layered framework for error detection. The framework combines schema and provenance checks, physical admissibility (bounds, symmetry, and governing equations), cross-source statistical consensus, model auditing, and suspicion-ranked review. In a production run, our verification gate halted 402 of 816 candidate values with typed reasons. Yet, an audit against curated references showed that 30 of 112 accepted values were defective; standard symmetry rules alone caught 21 of these. On measured BaTiO3 and KNbO3 tensors, constitutive identities caught 8 of 10 single-value errors and isolated the corrupted entries. In a controlled benchmark, the combined framework caught 81% of errors at 85% precision, including errors in single-report materials, bringing model accuracy on held-out data to within 3% of a model trained on clean data. Uncleaned data severely impairs discovery: 89% of the twenty largest values were errors, causing AI searches to prioritize false positives. Once bad numbers are controlled, missing measurement conditions emerge as the main limit, as distinct records become indistinguishable without full context. We outline directions for the field, including shared physics rule libraries and self-reporting databases.

infographic.key_insight: Rejecting suspect literature-mined values can protect AI materials discovery from false leads more effectively than retaining erroneous data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Layered data validation helps materials-screening models prioritize credible candidates rather than extraction artifacts.
method: Check schema, provenance, and physical admissibility.
Combine cross-source statistical consensus with model auditing.
Rank suspicious records for targeted review.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a controlled benchmark, the combined framework detected 81% of errors at 85% precision and brought held-out model accuracy within 3% of a clean-data-trained model.

infographic.paper_title: No Value Is Better Than a Wrong Value: Finding and Handling Erroneous Data in Literature-Mined Datasets for AI

title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials
authors: Sarath Menon, Braulio Sanchez Ortega, Ralf Drautz
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations with near \textit{ab initio} accuracy over large length and time scales. Foundation models extend this capability across the periodic table but inherit the thermodynamic description of the electronic structure methods used to generate their training data. Small errors in relative phase stability can therefore produce large errors in transformation temperatures. We introduce an additive thermodynamic correction layer that shifts phase free energies towards an assessed reference without retraining or modifying the base potential. A first order thermodynamic construction converts the required phase free energy shifts directly into configuration energy targets, which are fitted using a linear atomic cluster expansion and refined iteratively from measured free energies. We apply the method to melting and solid to solid transformations across elements with different crystal structures using a foundation GRACE model. After the correction, all transformation temperatures lie within the prescribed tolerance of the assessed values, including Ca, Ti, and Zr, where a solid to solid transition and melting are corrected together. Static energy curves, bulk moduli, and liquid structure remain close to those of the base model. Vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density depend on the corrected phase balance and change where the correction is large. The method requires neither retraining, differentiable dynamics, nor access to the parameters of the base potential. It provides a modular route for combining transferable atomistic models with assessed phase thermodynamics.

infographic.key_insight: An additive thermodynamic correction layer aligns machine learning interatomic potentials with assessed phase stability without retraining the base model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables more accurate melting and solid-state transformation temperatures while retaining transferable atomistic models.
method: Convert required phase free-energy shifts into configuration energy targets using a first-order thermodynamic construction.
Fit an additive linear atomic cluster expansion correction.
Refine the correction iteratively using measured free energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: With a foundation GRACE model, all tested transformation temperatures reached prescribed tolerances, including joint solid–solid and melting corrections for Ca, Ti, and Zr.
infographic.watch_item: Large corrections can change vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density, requiring validation beyond transition temperatures.
infographic.paper_title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials

title: Exploring Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Representation Learning of Powder X-ray Diffraction Patterns
authors: Ming-Chiang Chang, Brian DeCost
abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the primary high-throughput method for resolving crystal structures, a cornerstone of materials science. As high-throughput synthesis and self-driving laboratories advance, automated XRD pattern analysis has become vital for accelerating materials discovery. However, traditional matrix factorization methods fail when lattice variations cause non-linear peak shifts. At the same time, supervised learning approaches face a combinatorial explosion when handling multi-phase mixtures. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to learn representation embeddings from 1D diffraction patterns. By optimizing a masked self-prediction loss directly within the latent space, the framework captures high-level crystallographic semantics. Downstream evaluations show that lightweight attentive probes trained on frozen JEPA representations achieve space group classification and lattice parameter estimation accuracy close to much larger supervised vision transformers. Furthermore, latent probing reveals that the learned representation space naturally organizes physical transformations, isolating smooth trajectories for peak broadening. Interestingly, decoding along latent paths between single-phase crystal representations yields realistic multi-phase mixture patterns, demonstrating an emergent continuous structure learned without explicit multi-phase supervision.

infographic.key_insight: Self-supervised JEPA learns XRD representations that support crystal-property prediction and reveal continuous structure in peak broadening and multi-phase mixtures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusable XRD embeddings could support automated diffraction analysis for high-throughput materials discovery without requiring explicit supervision for every phase combination.
method: Learn representations from 1D diffraction patterns using masked prediction in latent space.
Train lightweight attentive probes on frozen embeddings for space group classification and lattice parameter estimation.

title: diff-soup: GPU-native Differentiable Simulation and Inference for Large-scale Stiff Dynamical Systems
authors: Samuel Degnan-Morgenstern, Martin Z. Bazant
abstract: Learning physical models from spatiotemporal data requires simulating systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) and differentiating through their solution. Upon spatial discretization, these models give rise to stiff dynamical systems that require repeatedly solving large, sparse linear systems. Traditional scientific computing frameworks are largely CPU-based and require problem-specific tuning to accelerate, scale, and differentiate. In this work, we introduce diff-soup, a differentiable, sparse-oriented, unified PDE suite for GPU-native simulation and inference of large, stiff dynamical systems. Built in JAX, diff-soup provides 1) a fully differentiable design for problems with sparse structure, 2) scaling to large problems through the NVIDIA cuDSS sparse direct solver with model and data multi-GPU parallelism, and 3) end-to-end PDE-constrained optimization, from classical statistical inference to embedded deep learning. On stiff PDE benchmarks, diff-soup outperforms established CPU- and GPU-based frameworks by one to two orders of magnitude in both forward solves and gradients. We demonstrate both a classical Bayesian inference workflow, identifying constitutive relationships, and a modern deep learning workflow, training a neural field for the catalyst activity of a three-dimensional packed bed reactor. We provide diff-soup as an open-source repository to facilitate research in computational science and engineering.

infographic.key_insight: diff-soup enables GPU-native, differentiable simulation and inference for large, stiff PDE systems, reporting 10–100× speedups in forward solves and gradients on benchmarks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It can accelerate physics-based parameter inference and learned constitutive models, including spatial catalyst-activity estimation in three-dimensional reactors.
method: Uses JAX for end-to-end differentiation of sparse PDE simulations.
Integrates NVIDIA cuDSS sparse direct solves with model and data multi-GPU parallelism.
Supports PDE-constrained Bayesian inference and embedded neural-field training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons against established CPU and GPU frameworks on stiff PDE benchmarks, plus constitutive-relation inference and a 3D packed-bed reactor neural-field demonstration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on sparse-system structure and GPU resources; the abstract does not specify benchmark sizes or hardware configurations.
infographic.paper_title: diff-soup: GPU-native Differentiable Simulation and Inference for Large-scale Stiff Dynamical Systems

title: Phase field dislocation dynamics prediction of stacking fault widths in Cu-Al Alloys using generalised stacking fault energy from DFT and interatomic potentials
authors: Arjun Varma R., Ankosh D. Deshmukh, Sushil Kumar, Vaishali Shah, M. P. Gururajan
abstract: The equilibrium width of intrinsic stacking faults is an important material parameter affecting key deformation phenomena. Here, we perform a comparative assessment of $γ$-surfaces generated using MD -- with a classical embedded-atom potential (ZW) and a machine-learned Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) -- and density functional theory (DFT), for Cu-Al alloys of varying Al content, and incorporate them as an energy term in PFDD simulations to obtain the equilibrium SFW. All three methods reproduce the lattice parameter and elastic moduli of Cu and Cu-Al alloys in reasonable agreement with each other and with experimental measurements from literature, but the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces, for both ZW and GAP, deviate substantially from DFT at the seven characteristic points, with the largest discrepancies at $T$ and $T_1$. When incorporated into PFDD, the DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces successfully predict an equilibrium SFW that increases with Al content and agrees well with standalone MD measurements and experimental values for pure Cu, whereas the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces do not yield an accurate SFW within PFDD, as the altered generalized stacking fault energy landscape causes the dissociating partials to become pinned soon after separation. These results show that DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces remain the more reliable route to alloy SFW prediction, and interatomic potentials must capture the shear path accurately to enable robust, efficient MD-PFDD modelling of stacking faults in alloys.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-derived stacking-fault energy landscapes enable reliable PFDD predictions of Cu–Al stacking-fault widths, while landscapes from the tested classical and machine-learned potentials cause premature partial-dislocation pinning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate alloy deformation modelling requires potentials that reproduce the shear-energy landscape, not just lattice parameters and elastic moduli.
method: Compare generalized stacking-fault energy surfaces from DFT, classical embedded-atom ZW, and machine-learned GAP methods.
Incorporate each energy surface into phase field dislocation dynamics (PFDD) simulations.
Evaluate equilibrium stacking-fault widths across Al contents against standalone MD and available experimental values.
infographic.evidence_signal: Despite reasonable agreement in lattice parameters and elastic moduli, both potentials deviate substantially from DFT at characteristic energy-surface points; DFT-driven PFDD predicts widths that increase with Al content and agree with standalone MD and pure-Cu experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental agreement reported in the abstract is limited to pure Cu, so validation across Cu–Al compositions remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Phase field dislocation dynamics prediction of stacking fault widths in Cu-Al Alloys using generalised stacking fault energy from DFT and interatomic potentials

title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors
authors: Zixu Huang, Julisa Juarez, Akash Dasgupta, David S. Ginger
abstract: Buried interfaces play a critical role in the operational stability of perovskite optoelectronic devices, yet remain challenging to probe non-destructively. Here, we demonstrate a multiwavelength photoluminescence-based approach exploiting the wavelength-dependent absorption of perovskites, enabling fast, and non-destructive probing of depth-sensitive degradation behavior of perovskite devices under operational conditions. Using ultraviolet (UV) light-soaking with different indium tin oxide (ITO) modifiers as a test case, we employ wide-field photoluminescence (PL) imaging, time-resolved photoluminescence (trPL) and ideality factor measurements with different wavelength excitation to characterize degradation behavior of both perovskite thin films and photovoltaic devices under UV soaking. Using only nondestructive characterization, we show that UV-induced degradation in p-i-n perovskite solar cells occurs preferentially at the HTL interface, adversely affecting device stability, consistent with ex-situ destructive tests. Our results also show that modifying the buried interface with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane reduces UV-induced damage at the buried interface, thus improving the UV stability of both perovskite films and devices. This work establishes a fast, non-destructive strategy to screen depth-dependent degradation in perovskite devices, offering insights for interface design and stability optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Multiwavelength photoluminescence non-destructively reveals depth-dependent UV degradation in perovskite devices, identifying preferential damage at the buried hole-transport-layer interface.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables rapid screening of buried-interface treatments to improve the UV stability of perovskite solar cells.
method: Use wavelength-dependent absorption to probe different depths with photoluminescence.
Combine wide-field PL imaging, time-resolved PL, and ideality-factor measurements during UV-soaking studies.
Compare perovskite films and devices with different indium tin oxide surface modifiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nondestructive measurements localized UV damage consistently with ex-situ destructive tests and showed reduced damage and improved UV stability with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane modification.
infographic.watch_item: Depth sensitivity depends on wavelength-dependent absorption; the abstract does not establish quantitative depth resolution or generality beyond the tested UV-soaking conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors

title: Machine learning enabled design of sustainable alloys considering real world constraints
authors: Quan Li, Zhilong Wang, Lei Shi, Baojing Feng, Changhui Liu, Jie Wang
abstract: Designing sustainable alloys must reconcile high performance with real-world constraints, including feedstock scarcity and variability, processing and energy requirements, regulatory thresholds, and economic limitations. Addressing these constraints reaches far beyond today's conventional performance-focused frameworks. It needs to consider not only complex property-processing-performance trade-offs but also sustainable production pathways. Here, we propose a physics-informed ensemble (PIE) learning framework that integrates fundamental structure-property relationships with processing routes and sustainability criteria for mechanism-based alloy design. It predicts properties from composition-microstructure relationships and infers processing routes under sustainability constraints, establishing an interdisciplinary approach to identifying sustainable alloy solutions. We validate the approach for Mg alloys, a lightweight yet energy-intensive metallic material class, considering performance, cost, and carbon emissions. Trained on a benchmark dataset, the PIE model systematically explores plausible alloy compositions and microstructures to construct a digital library of millions of candidate alloys. From this space, we identify two sustainable Mg alloy solutions that overcome the conventional performance-cost-emission trade-off: a rare-earth-containing alloy increases yield and tensile strength by 72.8 percent and 61.1 percent, respectively, over alloys from the same family at comparable cost and emissions; and a rare-earth-free alloy reduces cost and carbon emissions by 40.4 percent and 88.9 percent, respectively, relative to its primary-feedstock counterpart, without compromising mechanical performance. This work introduces a general, physics-informed, and quantifiable framework for designing sustainable alloys under real-world constraints.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed ensemble learning identifies Mg alloys that improve strength or reduce cost and carbon emissions under real-world sustainability constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links composition, microstructure, and processing routes to help engineers balance mechanical performance with feedstock, cost, and emissions constraints.
method: Integrate structure–property relationships, processing routes, and sustainability criteria in a physics-informed ensemble model.
Train on a benchmark dataset and generate a digital library of millions of candidate alloys.
Identify Mg alloy solutions balancing strength, cost, and carbon emissions.

title: Transition Metal-Anchored Newly Synthesized Aza-Triphenylene Monolayer for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction: Insights from DFT
authors: Soumendra Kumar Das, Jagannath Pradhan, Prasanjit Samal, Sridhar Sahu, Brahmananda Chakraborty
abstract: First-principles calculations were employed to explore the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity in two-dimensional aza-triphenylene monolayers functionalized with transition metals. Among the various metals studied, Co, Ru, and Y demonstrate outstanding catalytic efficacy, lowering the hydrogen adsorption free energy from -0.78 eV for pure aza-triphenylene to 0.05, 0.20, and 0.06 eV, respectively. Volcano plot analysis corroborates their enhanced HER activity. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations confirm thermal stability, while the electronic structure and charge transfer analysis reveal the strong catalyst-surface interaction. Metal decoration also improves the carrier mobility, particularly for Ru-functionalized aza-triphenylene. The climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for Co-functionalized aza-triphenylene exhibit activation barriers of 1.61, 2.29, and 5.88 eV for the Volmer, Heyrovsky, and Tafel reactions, respectively, highlighting a preferred Volmer-Heyrovsky route with the Heyrovsky being the rate-determining step. These findings highlight the potential of transition-metal-functionalized aza-triphenylene as a promising platform for developing efficient HER electrocatalysts.

infographic.key_insight: DFT calculations predict that anchoring Co, Ru, or Y on aza-triphenylene improves hydrogen adsorption energetics toward the near-zero values desirable for hydrogen evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Metal-functionalized aza-triphenylene offers a computationally identified platform for designing two-dimensional HER electrocatalysts.
method: First-principles DFT and HER volcano-plot analysis
Ab initio molecular dynamics and electronic-structure analysis
Climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations of reaction barriers
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted hydrogen adsorption free energies shift from −0.78 eV for pristine aza-triphenylene to 0.05, 0.20, and 0.06 eV with Co, Ru, and Y, respectively; Co reaction barriers favor a Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation is needed, and the predicted 2.29 eV Heyrovsky barrier for Co suggests a kinetic limitation despite favorable adsorption energetics.
infographic.paper_title: Transition Metal-Anchored Newly Synthesized Aza-Triphenylene Monolayer for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction: Insights from DFT

title: Charge density-supervised real-space representations for atomistic energy prediction
authors: Heting Liao, Masato Wakeda, Takahito Ohmura
abstract: Ground-state electron density contains sufficient information to determine ground-state energy, while providing spatial electronic information. This study developed a charge-density-informed graph neural network (hereafter CDGNN) that jointly learns energy and valence electron density from equivariant atomic graphs. This approach incorporates density-supervised real-space probe representations into the global energy regressor, allowing density-related spatial information to contribute to energy prediction. On the QM9 dataset, CDGNN reduced the energy prediction errors relative to an equivariant GNN baseline for interpolation and extrapolation to larger molecules. For small H-containing Fe and Fe-C datasets, CDGNN performed similarly to the baseline, indicating the dataset-dependent benefits of density supervision. CDGNN also accurately predicted the charge density distributions for molecular and Fe-based systems. The attention analysis showed higher weights for probe representations near the H atoms in Fe-based structures. These findings highlight the potential of integrating charge-density information for energy prediction and its task-dependent benefits.

infographic.key_insight: Supervising real-space representations with electron density improved molecular energy prediction, but gains depended on the dataset.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Charge-density-informed models could improve atomistic energy prediction while providing spatial electronic information for materials analysis.
method: Train an equivariant graph neural network jointly on energy and valence electron density.
Integrate density-supervised real-space probe representations into the global energy regressor.
Analyze attention weights to identify influential probe locations.
infographic.evidence_signal: CDGNN reduced energy errors versus an equivariant GNN baseline on QM9 interpolation and larger-molecule extrapolation, matched baseline performance on small H-containing Fe and Fe-C datasets, and accurately predicted density distributions.
infographic.watch_item: Density supervision requires electron-density training data and does not guarantee improved energy accuracy across material systems.
infographic.paper_title: Charge density-supervised real-space representations for atomistic energy prediction
